# Ritchie language capsule

> The complete description of the Ritchie programming language as the current compiler implements it. It is the capsule of the Ritchie Agent Skill, version 2026-11-24-7b90e549, and the text of https://ritchie.dev/tech/ritchie-at-a-glance/. The site index for coding agents is https://ritchie.dev/llms.txt.

Every claim about Ritchie comes from the language capsule below, not
from any other language. For a facility the capsule lacks, say that
the skill does not document it and offer a documented alternative.

## Writing programs

Prefer the smallest program that answers the request, and explain the
constructs a reader may not know. Check every program you present with the
compiler until it prints what it should, and call any unchecked program
unchecked.

## Running programs

Programs run with the Ritchie compiler, whose commands are `ritchie`,
`rcc`, and `rcrun`, and with Go 1.27 or newer, which builds them. If `rcrun`
is not on `PATH`, ask the user before installing it. On macOS or Linux, this
puts the commands in
`~/.local/bin`:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://ritchie.dev/install.sh | sh
```

Windows archives and the licence are at https://ritchie.dev/downloads/releases/.
In a checkout of the Ritchie source, install from its root instead:

```sh
go -C src install ./cmd/ritchie
cp src/bin/rcc src/bin/rcrun "$(dirname "$(command -v ritchie)")"
```

`rcrun --diagnostics=jsonl -` runs the source on standard input.
`rcc dir/solution.ri` compiles without running and writes into the current
directory the bundle `solution.run`, which `rcrun solution.run` runs, for a
program that declares a service, and the executable `solution` otherwise.

`RITCHIE_LOG_LEVEL` selects what a run writes to standard error and changes
nothing else: `0` nothing; `1`, the default, `log` output, diagnostics, and
the report of an error that escapes `main`; `2` and `3` also the errors that
leave service methods and handler arms.

- Exit status 1 with only JSON lines on standard error: the compiler
  rejected the source.
- Exit status 1 after program output: an error escaped `main`, and its
  report follows on standard error with `at` and `raised by` lines.

## Serving services over HTTP

`rcrun --serve program.ri` runs `main`, if any, and serves every service
method over HTTP at `127.0.0.1:7824`, or with `--serve=8080` on port 8080,
until it receives a signal.

Each method is reached at `POST /{module}/{Service}/{method}`, where the
module is the file name without `.ri`. The request carries
`Content-Type: application/json` and a JSON object with a property for each
parameter, keyed by its name. An array is a JSON array, and a dictionary is
a JSON array of objects such as `{"key": "a", "value": 2}`. A successful
call returns status 200 and the result as JSON.

```ritchie
UnknownSku! { String sku }

@Orders {}

@Orders.total(String[] skus, Int[] qtys) -> Int | UnknownSku! {
    Int sum = 0
    for i in range(count(skus)) {
        if skus[i] != "pear" { return UnknownSku! { sku: skus[i] } }
        sum += 5 * qtys[i]
    }
    return sum
}

main() {
    print(@Orders.total(["pear"], [2]))
}
```

Posted to `http://127.0.0.1:7824/program/Orders/total`, the body
`{"skus": ["pear", "pear"], "qtys": [2, 1]}` gets `15`, and
`{"skus": ["kiwi"], "qtys": [1]}` gets status 422,
`Content-Type: application/problem+json`, and this body:

```json
{"type":"urn:ritchie:error:UnknownSku","title":"UnknownSku!","status":422,"detail":"UnknownSku! { sku: \"kiwi\" }","ritchieFields":{"sku":"kiwi"}}
```

Any error that leaves the method gets status 422 in this form, and a built-in
error such as `OutOfRange!` has no `ritchieFields`. A body that is not JSON,
lacks a parameter without a default, has a property that is not a parameter,
or holds a value outside the parameter's type, such as `40000` for an
`Int16` or 4 elements for an `Int[3]`, gets status 400 with the `Malformed!`
problem body. A `Float` takes any JSON number, a `Decimal` a number or a
string, keeping its written scale, and a `Date`, `Time`, or `Duration` a
string such as `"2026-03-02"`, `"23:30:00"`, or `"90.5s"`, which results and
`ritchieFields` use too.

Requests run concurrently, each under its own time budget, and one still
running when its budget ends gets 504 with the `Cancelled!` problem body.

## Teaching

Teach one idea at a time in capsule order with short programs you have run,
ask the learner to predict or change something small, give a hint before a
solution, and explain the rule behind a diagnostic.

## Language capsule

### Program basics

- Source files use the `.ri` extension, and comments are `//` and
  `/* ... */`. An executable has one `main()` with no parameters, no
  result, and no error list.
- Newlines end statements, and semicolons separate statements on one line.
  A statement continues onto the next line only inside parentheses, square
  brackets, or the braces of a construction, so a line break beside a
  binary operator needs enclosing parentheses.
- Values and functions start lowercase, one-letter ones too, so `Int N = 1`
  is rejected with `name.unexpected-class`. Types and services start
  uppercase and contain a lowercase letter, as in `@Db`, and constants are
  all uppercase with at least two characters, such as `MAX_N`.
- Every variable and constant is declared with its type, as in
  `String DIGITS = "0123"`, not `DIGITS = "0123"`. Module level declares
  constants of any type, such as `[String: Int] RANK`, but no variables, so
  a lowercase name there is rejected with `name.unexpected-class`.
- Boolean operators are `and`, `or`, and `not`, and `and` and `or` skip
  the right operand when the left decides, as in `i < n and xs[i] > 0`.
  `&&`, `||`, `!x`, `++`, and `--` do not exist; write `n += 1`.
- Precedence, tightest first: member access, call, index; unary `-`; `*` `/`
  `%`; `+` `-`; `??`; `<` `<=` `>` `>=`; `==` `!=`; `not`; `and`; `or`;
  `c ? a : b`, which does not nest. A chain such as `a < b <= c` holds
  when each neighbouring pair holds, and one that mixes `<` and `>` forms
  is rejected.
- `print(v)` writes `v` and a line break to standard output, and `log(v)` to
  standard error.
- A local variable that is not read is a compile error; a loop variable or
  a parameter may stay unread.
- Keywords cannot be names, locals included: `and any break case contract
  continue create else embed exhaustive false for handle if in is match
  none not or resume return self then true unique where`.

### Variables and functions

```ritchie
Int LIMIT = 42

double(Int value) -> Int { return value * 2 }
pair() -> (Int, Bool) { return 1, true }
greet(String name, String greeting = "hello") -> String {
    return f"{greeting} {name}"
}

main() {
    Int total = double(LIMIT)
    Int left, right = 1, 2
    Int n, Bool ok = pair()
    Int later
    later = left + right
    String who = greet(name: "ada")
    print(f"{total} {n} {ok} {later} {who}")
}
```

A call written as a statement discards its results. A declaration binds every
result, so `Int n = pair()` is rejected with `variable.arity`, and each of its
variables, `_` too, must be read. A variable must be assigned on every path
before it is read. Arguments are all positional or all named.

Function types are written `(Int, Int) -> Int`. A closure is written with
`=>` and captures copies of the variables it uses:

```ritchie
apply(Int x, (Int) -> Int f) -> Int { return f(x) }

main() {
    Int offset = 10
    (Int) -> Int add = x => x + offset
    print(apply(1, add))
    print(apply(2, x => x * x))
    (Int, Int) -> Int plus = (a, b) => a + b
    print(plus(3, 4))
}
```

### Numbers

- `Int` is 64-bit. `Int8`, `Int16`, and `Int32` widen to wider integers.
  Integer `/` truncates toward zero, `%` takes the dividend's sign, and
  division by zero raises `DivisionByZero!`.
- `Float` is binary64. `print` and an f-string slot write the shortest
  text that reads back as the same value, so `198.0` prints `198` and
  `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004`, in exponent form from an
  exponent of 6 or below -4, as in `1.5e+07` and `1e-05`.
- `Decimal` is exact decimal arithmetic that keeps the written scale. A
  literal with a fraction part, such as `0.00`, is a `Decimal` where a
  `Decimal` is required and a `Float` otherwise: after `Decimal a = 1.20`,
  `print(a + 3.400)` prints `4.600`, `Decimal b = 1.25 * 3.00` holds
  `3.7500`, and `print(1.20 + 3.400)` prints the `Float` `4.6`.
- Integers, Floats, and Decimals do not mix in arithmetic or comparisons,
  so convert with `Float.fromInt(n)`, `Decimal.fromInt(n)`, or
  `Int.fromFloat(x)`, which truncates toward zero.
- A `Byte` holds 0 to 255. `Byte.fromInt(n)` and `Int.fromByte(b)` convert,
  `Byte[].fromString(s)` gives the UTF-8 bytes of `s`, and
  `String.fromBytes(bs)` decodes them, raising `Malformed!` for invalid
  UTF-8.

### Conditions, match, and loops

```ritchie
grade(Int score) -> String {
    match {
        case score >= 90 => { return "A" }
        any => { return "C" }
    }
}

main() {
    print(grade(85))
}
```

`if c { } else if d { } else { }` takes no parentheses. A `match` with a
subject compares it with each `case` value, such as a literal or a constant,
and one without tries each `case` condition, in order. The first selected arm
runs, in braces, and `any` is the remainder. A `match` that lists every enum
member does not count as returning on every path, so when its arms return,
write the last member as `any`.

```ritchie
main() {
    for i in range(3) { print(i) }             // 0, 1, 2
    for i in range(2, 8, 3) { print(i) }       // 2, 5
    for x in [10, 20] { print(x) }
    for k, v in ["a": 1] { print(f"{k}={v}") }
    Int n = 0
    for n < 3 { n += 1 }
    outer: for r in range(3) {
        for c in range(3) {
            if r + c == 3 { break outer }
        }
    }
}
```

`for { }` loops until `break`. `break` and `continue`, also in a `match`
arm, act on the innermost loop, and `break name` or `continue name` act on
the loop labelled `name:`.

### Structs, methods, and enums

```ritchie
Point {
    Int x
    Int y = 0
}

Point.shift(Int dx) {
    self.x += dx
}

Figure { CIRCLE, SQUARE }

main() {
    Point p = Point { x: 1 }
    p.shift(4)
    print(p)
    Figure s = Figure.SQUARE
    match s {
        case Figure.CIRCLE => { print("round") }
        case Figure.SQUARE => { print("square") }
    }
    print(s)
}
```

This prints `Point { x: 5, y: 0 }` first and `SQUARE` last. A method that
uses `self` may change its receiver when that is a variable, a field, or an
element, so `counters[i].advance()` updates the array. A method without
`self` is called through its type, as in `Point.origin()`. Assigning,
passing, or returning a struct copies it. A struct contains itself only
through a nullable field, an array, or a dictionary, such as
`Node? next = none`.

### Arrays

```ritchie
main() {
    Int[] xs = [3, 1, 2]
    xs = append(xs, 4)
    xs[0] = 9
    print(xs[1:3])
    print(sort(xs))
}
```

Array operations are free functions: `count`, `contains`, `indexOf` (an
`Int?`), `first` and `last` (nullable), `append`, `insert(xs, i, v)`,
`removeAt(xs, i)`, `concat`, `reverse`, `sort`, and `fill(v, n)`. No array
function changes its argument, so `sort(xs)` alone does nothing: write
`xs = sort(xs)` and `xs = append(xs, v)`. An empty literal `[]` needs a
declared type. `grid[r][c] = 0` assigns one element of an `Int[][]`.
`Int[3]` holds exactly 3 elements and is a type apart from `Int[]`, which
its slice `k[0:3]` is. A module constant `Int[] MISS = [-1]` acts as an
`Int[1]` in a handler arm, `append`, and `==`, so bind
`Int[] miss = MISS` first. Slices `xs[lo:hi]` are half-open, and
indexing out of range raises `OutOfRange!`. `map`, `filter`, `reduce`,
`sum`, `find`, and `sortBy` do not exist, and `+` and `+=` do not apply to
arrays.

An index or key in an assignment target is a variable or its field, a
literal, or `+`, `-`, or `*` of them. Any other, such as an element or its
field, a slice, `/`, `%`, an f-string, or a call such as `toLower(w)`, as in
`d[f[0]] = 1`, is rejected with `assignment.fallible-operand`, so bind it to
a variable first. A read takes any index or key.

Assigning an element or entry, also through `self`, and assigning the result
of `append`, `concat`, `insert`, `removeAt`, or `remove` to the same
variable, field, element, or entry change the value in place, as in
`xs = removeAt(xs, count(xs) - 1)` and `d[k] = append(d[k], v)`, and
`for i in range(n)` builds no array. A function copies an array or
dictionary parameter at each call only when it assigns to it, and the caller
sees the change only through a returned value. A slice and `s = f"{s}..."`
copy the whole value, so repeating them on a large value takes quadratic
time: collect strings in an array for `join`.

### Strings

```ritchie
main() {
    String[] names = []
    for name in split("usr/local/bin", "/") {
        names = append(names, replace(name, "l", "L"))
    }
    print(join(reverse(names), " < "))
    String word = "hello"
    Int at, Bool found = indexOf(word, "l")
    print(f"{at} {found} {count(word)} {word[1:3]}")
}
```

- String operations are free functions that take the string first:
  `count`, `isEmpty`, `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `indexOf`,
  `toUpper` and `toLower`, which also convert non-ASCII letters, `trim`,
  `replace(s, old, new)`, `split(s, sep)`, and `join(parts, sep)`. `split`
  keeps empty fields: `split("a  b", " ")` is `["a", "", "b"]`, and
  `split("", " ")` is `[""]`.
- An f-string slot cannot contain a string literal, so `f"{join(xs, "/")}"`
  is rejected with `interpolation.unterminated`: bind `String sep = "/"`
  first. Doubled braces write a literal brace. `+` does not join strings.
- Positions and counts are UTF-8 bytes. `s[i]` is rejected, and a slice
  whose start or end falls inside a character raises
  `InvalidStringBoundary!`: for `String s = "é!"`, `count(s)` is 3, `s[0:1]`
  raises it, and `s[2:3]` is `!`. `split(s, "")` gives the characters,
  `["é", "!"]`, whose `count` is 2.
- `<`, `>`, `==`, and `sort` order strings by their UTF-8 bytes, so
  `"Z" < "a"` and `"é" > "z"`.
- Quoted strings take escapes such as `\n`, `\t`, and `\"`, and a backtick
  string is raw and may span lines.
- `Int.fromString(s)` accepts a sign and digits, so `"075"` gives `75`, and
  raises `Malformed!` for other text, such as `" 5"`.

### Dictionaries and nullable values

```ritchie
main() {
    [String: Int] ages = ["ada": 36]
    String[] f = split("lin 41", " ")
    String who = f[0]
    ages[who] = Int.fromString(f[1])  // not ages[f[0]]
    ages["ada"] = (ages.get("ada") ?? 0) + 1
    print(ages["ada"])
    Int? maybe = ages.get("bo")
    if maybe {
        print(maybe)
    } else {
        print("absent")
    }
}
```

`[K: V]` is a dictionary and `[:]` is an empty one. `d[k]` raises
`MissingKey!` for a missing key, `d.get(k)` returns `V?`, and `has`, `keys`,
`values`, `remove`, and `count` are free functions. Iteration and `keys`
have no fixed order. `T?` holds a `T` or `none`; test it with `if x` or
`x != none` before using it as `T`. A test that leaves the function, such as
`if v == none { return -1 }`, narrows `v` to `T` for the rest of the
function, so a later `v ?? 0` is rejected there.

### Errors

```ritchie
Low! { Int n }
High! {}

check(Int n) -> Int {
    if n < 0 { return Low! { n: n } }
    if n > 9 { return High! }
    return n
}

main() {
    Int a = check(-2) handle Low! e => e.n * 10
    Int b = check(20) handle {
        Low! => 0
        High! => 99
    }
    print(f"{a} {b}")
    for n in [1, -1, 50] {
        Int c = check(n) handle {
            Low! => continue
            High! => break
        }
        print(c)
    }
    print(check(-5))
}
```

Returning an error value raises it, also from `main` or a function without a
result, and a function's result type stays the success type. A function may
list its errors after the result with `|`, as in `-> Int | Low! | High!` or
`-> none | Low!`, and a function without a list may raise any error. A list
names every declared error type that can leave the function, its callees'
included, and no other (`contract.undeclared-error`,
`contract.unraised-error`), and a function that calls a function value cannot
have one. A function that returns nothing ends with a bare `return` or at its
end, and `return none` is rejected.

Built-in errors, such as `OutOfRange!`, `MissingKey!`, `Malformed!`,
`LengthMismatch!`, and the remote failures, form a catalog: declaring one
is rejected with `name.reserved-name`, no error list may name one, and
constructing one is rejected with `error.catalog-construction` except
under `rcc --debug`.

`handle` follows the whole statement it protects, not an argument or other
part of it, on the line where that statement ends. An arm replaces the
statement's whole value, such as the new `xs` of `xs = append(xs, f(n))`,
or runs `continue`, `break`, or `return`, `return E!` in an arm raises
another error, as in `Low! => return High!`, and `E! e` binds the error
when the arm reads it. A block arm, such as
`Low! e => { print(e.n); continue }`, supplies a replacement value by ending
with `resume value`. A handler after a block or a loop, with `handle` on the
line of the closing brace, protects each statement inside, so after an arm
that completes, the block continues with its next statement, and `continue`
and `break` in an arm of `for x in xs { ... } handle { ... }` act on that
loop. A variable that a protected statement assigns has a value after it
only when every arm that completes assigns it too, even when it held a
value before.

### Type aliases

`Name = Type` at module level gives a type a second name. An array of a
function type needs an alias, as in `Step = (Int) -> Int` and
`Step[] steps = [x => x + 1]`. A nullable function value such as `Step?`
cannot be tested, compared with `none`, or called, so pass a function with
the default behavior instead.

### Services

A service is declared as `@Name {}`, and its methods have no `self`, take
defaults and list errors like a function, and are called as
`@Name.method(...)`. Their parameters and results are built-in types,
structs and enums that have a method whose name does not start with `_`, and
arrays and dictionaries of them; any other type is rejected with
`service.boundary-type`. Over HTTP a struct is a JSON object of its fields
and an enum the name of its member, as in `"GREEN"`.

### Clock, durations, and random numbers

A `Duration` literal is an integer with a unit, `ns`, `us`, `ms`, `s`, `m`,
`h`, or `d`, such as `1500ms`; `1.5s` is rejected.

`r::Clock.sleep(300ms)` suspends the caller, and
`r::Clock.time()` returns the current `DateTime`. `DateTime.fromUnix(n)` is
the instant `n` seconds after 1970-01-01 UTC, which prints as
`2026-03-02T11:00:00Z`, and `t.withOffset(330m)` prints the same instant as
`2026-03-02T16:30:00+05:30`. `t + d` adds a `Duration`, `t - u` gives one, and
`n * 1s` makes one, which prints its nonzero parts, as in `1d9h30m` or
`505ms33us`, and `0s` for zero. Dividing two durations gives a `Float`, so
`Int.fromFloat(d / 1ms)` is the count of milliseconds.

A `Date` is written and printed as `d2026-03-02` and a `Time` of day as
`t23:30:00.5`, and `f"{d}"[1:]` drops the letter. A `Time` wraps at
midnight under `+` and `-` of a `Duration`, `t01:00:00 - t23:30:00` is
`-22h30m`, and `t23:30:00.until(t01:00:00)` is `1h30m`. A `Date` has
`addDays(n)`, `addYears(n)`, `daysUntil(other)`, an `Int`, and
`addMonths(n)`, which gives `d2026-02-28` for `d2026-01-31.addMonths(1)`.
For a date's parts `y`, `m`, and `d`, the month's first day is
`Date f = d0001-01-01.addYears(y - 1).addMonths(m - 1)`, its length
`f.daysUntil(f.addMonths(1))` bounds a valid `d`, and the date is
`f.addDays(d - 1)`.

`r::Random g = r::Random.seed(s)` makes a generator whose draws are the
same for the same `Byte[32] s`, and `r::Random.new()` makes an unseeded one.
`g.range(lo, hi)` draws an `Int` in `[lo, hi)`,
`g.ratio()` a `Float` in `[0, 1)`, and `g.bits()` a 64-bit `BitSet`, which
prints as `0x` and 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits and can key a
dictionary. A literal such as `0` is a `BitSet` where one is required.
Assigning or passing a generator copies it, so a helper that draws returns
it, as in `-> (Int, r::Random)`, or draws through a struct field as
`self.g`. `Byte[32] s = fill(Byte.fromInt(0), 32)` makes a seed.

### Remote failures and the time budget

The runtime can fail a service call with a catalog error:
`Unavailable!`, `Rejected!`, `Conflict!`, `Unmodified!`, and `Cancelled!` mean
the call changed nothing, and `Unverified!` means a write may or may not have
happened. This example constructs `Unavailable!` itself to stand in for a
failing service, so it runs only as `rcrun --debug`.

```ritchie
@Weather {}

@Weather.reading(String station, Duration d) -> Int {
    if station == "north" { return Unavailable! }
    r::Clock.sleep(d)
    return 3
}

main() {
    Int a = @Weather.reading("north", 0ms) handle Unavailable! => -1
    Int c = @Weather.reading("west", 2500ms) handle Cancelled! => -2
    print(f"{a} {c}")
}
```

Every program runs under a time budget, 2000 ms by default, which limits
its service calls; other code, such as an `r::Clock.sleep` in `main`,
continues past it. `RITCHIE_ENTRY_BUDGET_MS` sets it for a run, and the
program text cannot set or read it. A service call starts only within the
first 70 percent of the budget, and a later one fails at once with
`Cancelled!`. A started call without a response when the budget ends fails
with `Cancelled!`, not `Unverified!`. Enforce time limits through this
budget and its errors, not by timing calls.

### Futures

A call of a service method starts where it is written, and the program
waits for its result at the first use of the value.

- Storing a result in a variable or an array element, or appending it to an
  array, does not wait when the target has the result's type, but a `T?`
  target for a `T` result waits. `count(xs)` of an array of results does
  not wait either. Every other use waits, such as a dictionary entry, a
  field, arithmetic, `if`, an argument of another call, and `print`.
- A use waits for its call and every call started before it, and so does a
  call of a function value. So of two failed calls the program sees the
  earlier one, and a loop whose body starts a call and also uses its result
  or calls a function value runs its calls in sequence. Collect the results
  in an array in one loop and use them in a second loop.
- A local routine whose body calls services, writes no output, has no
  `for` loop without `in`, and does not call itself, also through other
  routines, starts at its call in the same way, so a routine for one item,
  which may use its results and handle their failures, can be called for
  every item and the calls run together.
- A call's failure is raised at the call's statement, and only a handler
  there catches it; an arm on a later use that nothing else selects is
  rejected with `handle.dead-arm`.
- A handler whose arms are each a literal, a constant, or a variable, such
  as `handle Low! => 0`, or only return one, as in
  `handle Low! => { return 0 }`, does not wait, so a stored marker can
  stand for a failure. Any other arm, such as an f-string, waits.
- Leaving a routine waits for every call written before the exit and
  cancels every call written after it.
- A call with a side effect also starts early, so to start a call only after
  an earlier call has succeeded, use the earlier result first, as in an `if`.

```ritchie
Low!

@Gauge {}
@Gauge.level(Int id) -> Int | Low! {
    r::Clock.sleep(50ms)
    if id == 9 { return Low! }
    return id
}
@Gauge.trend(Int lv) -> Int { r::Clock.sleep(50ms); return lv * 2 }

reading(Int id) -> Int | Low! {
    Int lv = @Gauge.level(id)
    Int tr = @Gauge.trend(lv)
    return lv + tr
}

main() {
    Int[] sums = []
    for id in [1, 2, 3] {
        sums = append(sums, reading(id))
    }
    Int total = 0
    for s in sums { total += s }
    print(total)
    Int bad = reading(9) handle Low! => -1
    print(bad)
}
```

### Projects and modules

A project is a directory with `NAME.ritchie.toml`, whose `[modules]` table
maps each module to its directory, as in `stock = "stock"`. Every `.ri` file
under that directory belongs to the module, and at most one module declares
`main`. `rcc` with no file, run in the project directory, writes `NAME`, or
`NAME.run` when a service is declared.

`::` reaches another module, as in `stock::Item.find("pen")`,
`stock::Missing! e`, and `stock::@Depot.level("pen")`. Only a type with a
method whose name does not start with `_`, those methods, an error type and
its fields, and a service cross modules. Fields, struct literals, free
functions, and constants are rejected in another module with
`module.unpublished-member`. A served method's path names its module, as in
`/stock/Depot/level`.

## Known defects

The current compiler departs from the language in these forms, so write the
alternative.

- An enum that gives values to some members only crashes `rcc`, so give
  values to every member or to none.
- A struct field cannot hold a function, but `rcc` accepts one and can fail
  to build the program, so pass a function as a parameter or keep it in a
  variable, an array, or a dictionary.
